expected_evidence: geological: elevated carbon spherule / magnetic microspherule concentrations in a thin stratigraphic layer (Younger Dryas Boundary layer) across North American sedimentary sections
geological: associated platinum, iridium, or other siderophile-element anomalies in the same horizon
geological: nanodiamonds, melt-glass, and 'black mat' organic-rich layer directly above the spherule horizon
astronomical: physical impact crater or airburst structure (or absence thereof, consistent with an airburst rather than a ground impact)
astronomical/geological: charcoal and soot layers indicating continent-scale wildfires coincident with the horizon
material (archaeological): disruption or discontinuity in Clovis-era artifact assemblages and site occupation at ~10,950 BCE
material/faunal: megafaunal extinction signatures (bone beds, extinction horizon) clustering near the same date
genetic: population bottleneck signals in surviving North American megafauna or early human lineages dated to this interval
model_prior: published Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis literature (Firestone et al. 2007 and follow-up studies) reporting these proxies, alongside contested replication/rebuttal studies
response.rationale: The dated interval (~10,950 BCE) corresponds to the Younger Dryas onset boundary, so the 'younger-dryas' period row is the appropriate detectability baseline. The hypothesis (Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis) primarily predicts geological/geochemical evidence (carbon spherules, microspherules, platinum/iridium anomalies, nanodiamonds, black mat) which has a baseline detectability of 0.65, and companion astronomical evidence (crater/airburst structure or its diagnostic absence) at 0.7 — both relatively favorable because fine-grained sedimentary and ice-core records from this period are well preserved and widely sampled. Material (archaeological, 0.35) and genetic (0.3) evidence are less reliably detectable given poor preservation of organic/skeletal material over ~13,000 years and the difficulty of resolving fine-scale population bottlenecks. Textual and linguistic evidence are essentially inapplicable (0.0/0.05) since this predates writing and is far outside plausible oral-tradition retention. Given that carbon-spherule and microspherule layers matching this description have in fact been reported (per model-prior knowledge of the Firestone et al. 2007 YDIH literature and subsequent multi-site studies, though the impact-origin interpretation remains contested versus wildfire/other terrestrial explanations), I adjust the effective detectability for the dominant geological/astronomical evidence types slightly upward from the raw table average, to about 0.6, reflecting that this class of evidence is genuinely well-suited to survive and has already been the subject of active empirical search — an absence of geological anomalies would therefore be more informative against the hypothesis than absence of material or genetic evidence would be. This is a low-tier model-prior recollection, not a verified determination from the evidence text provided.
